meta.title: Greek A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Greek → English (see the Greek, recall the meaning) and English → Greek (see an English meaning, recall the Greek). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words of Modern Greek for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Greek has an examination at these levels, the Certificate of Attainment in Greek of the Centre for the Greek Language, but no graded word list for it was found published, so this deck is not that examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 313 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the articles, pronouns, question words, prepositions and particles every sentence is built out of — and the other 187 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Greek, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword has a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (spíti, tróo, the accent kept), so the deck can be studied before the alphabet is fluent; the Greek Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters themselves. The 182 nouns are printed with their article — ο, η or το — because the article is the gender, which every adjective, article and pronoun agrees with, and they show their genitive and plural; the 111 verbs show their simple past and future, where a Greek verb often changes stem (τρώω, έφαγα, θα φάω), and behind the All forms fold their present, simple past, imperfect, future and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 498 of the 500 words, three apiece for 491 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
